# minikv: snapshot-isolated transactions over a crash-safe write-ahead log

## What the task is

### Objective

`4612 / 20000 chars`

`/app` holds `minikv`, a small embedded key/value store written in pure
Python. It works, but it is naive: every `put` rewrites the entire database
file, there is no way to group changes into an atomic unit, and a process that
dies mid-write leaves an unreadable file behind.

Rebuild its storage engine so that it satisfies the specification in
`instruction.md`. Concretely, the finished store must provide:

1. **Snapshot-isolated transactions.** `db.begin()` returns a `Transaction`
   that reads a consistent snapshot of the committed state as of the moment
   `begin()` was called, plus its own uncommitted writes. Later commits by
   anyone else must be invisible to it, including for `scan()` — no phantoms.
   Opening a transaction must not block other writers; a single-threaded test
   opens a transaction, performs autocommit writes, and then reads through the
   transaction, so an implementation that holds a lock for the transaction's
   lifetime deadlocks.
2. **First-committer-wins conflict detection.** `commit()` raises
   `ConflictError` when any key in the transaction's *write set* was written
   after its snapshot was taken, by another transaction or by an autocommit
   call. Conflicts are computed on the write set only: a transaction that
   merely read a changed key still commits, so write skew is permitted and a
   test asserts it is permitted. A failed commit discards the whole write set
   and closes the transaction; using a closed transaction raises
   `TransactionClosedError`. `Transaction` is also a context manager that
   commits on a clean exit and rolls back on an exception.
3. **Durability against process death.** When `put`, `delete` or `commit()`
   returns, the change must already have reached the operating system: a
   `SIGKILL` on the next instruction must not lose it, and reopening the
   directory must show it. Writes from a transaction that never committed must
   never appear. The log must live in a single file named `wal.log` inside the
   database directory and must be the mechanism by which committed data
   reaches disk; its internal format is the author's choice.
4. **Recovery from a damaged log.** If `wal.log` is truncated at an arbitrary
   offset or any single byte in it is flipped, reopening must not raise, and
   the recovered state must be a *prefix* of the commit history: some commit
   `j` such that everything up to `j` is fully applied and nothing after it is
   applied even partially. Records therefore need a length and a checksum, and
   recovery must stop at the first record that fails to verify. A store
   reopened on a damaged log must also remain writable — new commits have to
   land where recovery will find them.
5. **Checkpointing.** `db.checkpoint()` folds the log into a compact
   representation. Afterwards `wal.log` must still exist and be at most 4 KiB,
   and the whole directory must be at most `4 * L + 65536` bytes where `L` is
   the sum of `len(key) + len(value)` over live keys — superseded versions and
   deleted keys have to actually be reclaimed. Checkpointing must be crash-safe
   (a `SIGKILL` during it cannot lose committed data) and must not change what
   an already-open transaction sees.
6. **Throughput.** With 16-byte keys and 96-byte values: 20 000 autocommit
   `put`s in under 20 s; 20 000 random `get`s after a `checkpoint()` in under
   5 s; 50 prefix scans over 20 000 keys through a transaction whose snapshot
   is already stale, in under 10 s; 2 000 single-write transactions in under
   10 s; and reopening a 10 000-commit log in under 15 s. Reads must stay fast
   on both paths — post-checkpoint and against an older snapshot — rather than
   degrading into a per-key search.
7. **Thread safety.** One `MiniKV` object shared by 8 threads doing autocommit
   writes to disjoint keys must lose, duplicate and corrupt nothing; threads
   each opening their own transaction over disjoint keys must all commit
   without spurious conflicts; and a transaction must keep seeing a consistent
   snapshot while other threads commit.

Done looks like: the 13 visible tests in `/app/public_tests` still pass, and
the sealed suite — 117 tests across seven categories — reaches the 0.85 pass
threshold; the reference reaches 1.0000.

Constraints: Python 3.11 standard library only, no network, and every file the
agent adds or changes must live inside `/app/minikv/` — grading copies
`minikv/**/*.py` into a clean tree and discards everything else, including any
edits to the visible tests. The store must not consult the environment, the
process tree, the call stack or test-runner state.

### Motivation

`1158 / 10000 chars`

Storage engines are where "looks correct" and "is correct" diverge the most.
Snapshot isolation, write-ahead logging and crash recovery are the three ideas
every real database is built on, and each of them has a plausible-looking wrong
version that passes a casual test suite: a snapshot that silently tracks the
latest state, a "durable" write that is still sitting in a Python buffer, a
recovery loop that resynchronises past a corrupt record and resurrects a commit
that was never made. An agent that can only pattern-match on the vocabulary
will write all three.

The scenario is ordinary professional work rather than a puzzle. There is a
real package with a real public API, callers that depend on its exception
names, an existing test suite that must keep passing, and a performance budget
that rules out the obvious shortcut — the situation an engineer is in when a
component that was "fine for now" has to become load-bearing. Getting it right
means holding an invariant across several files — version chains, conflict
windows, log framing, checkpoint ordering — and noticing where those
invariants interact, which is the capability worth measuring.

## Difficulty & effort

### Difficulty explanation

`3605 / 20000 chars`

The individual techniques are textbook; the difficulty is that they constrain
each other, and only a design that satisfies all of them at once survives the
sealed suite.

* **MVCC is forced, not optional.** The obvious way to make transactions look
  isolated is a lock held from `begin()` to `commit()`. The specification and
  the matching test rule that out from a single thread: open a transaction,
  run 50 autocommit writes, then read through the transaction. A held lock
  deadlocks, and a "snapshot" that is really a live view returns the new
  value. The agent has to keep per-key version chains and resolve reads at a
  version.
* **Conflict detection has to be exactly snapshot isolation.** Too weak and
  lost updates slip through; too strong — validating the read set, as in
  serializable snapshot isolation — and the write-skew test fails, because it
  asserts that a pair of transactions reading each other's keys and writing
  disjoint ones *both* commit. The suite tests both directions, so an agent
  that reaches for the strongest-sounding algorithm loses.
* **Durability is tested by actually killing the process.** Child processes
  `SIGKILL` themselves and the parent asserts the child died by signal 9;
  buffered writes with no `flush()` vanish, `close()` never runs, and any
  design that persists on close or at exit scores zero here.
* **Damaged-log recovery is the part that is easy to get subtly wrong.** The
  suite truncates the log at eight fractions and flips a byte at eight
  positions, then asserts the recovered state is a prefix of the commit
  history — no invented keys, no wrong values, no gaps. That needs per-record
  length *and* checksum, stopping at the first bad record rather than
  resynchronising, and a guard against a corrupted length field that would
  otherwise drive a huge read. A further test writes to the store *after*
  recovering from a truncated log and reopens again: an implementation that
  appends behind the damaged tail loses the new write silently. That is a bug
  the reference implementation actually had until the suite caught it.
* **Checkpointing has an ordering requirement.** Write the new snapshot
  atomically, then truncate the log — the other order loses data if the
  process dies between the two, and a crash test kills the process at a random
  moment inside a checkpoint loop. Recovery then has to ignore log records
  already folded into the snapshot, so versions must be comparable across the
  two files. Pruning the in-memory version chains has its own constraint:
  chains may only be trimmed below the oldest snapshot still held by an open
  transaction, or `checkpoint()` corrupts a transaction that is mid-flight.
* **The performance budget removes the escape hatch.** Rewriting a snapshot
  per commit satisfies every correctness test and misses the 20 000-put budget
  by orders of magnitude. Append-only is effectively mandatory, which is what
  makes the recovery requirements bite.
* **The visible tests do not describe the target.** They cover what the store
  already does. An agent that treats the shipped suite as the definition of
  done writes nothing at all and scores its floor; the specification is the
  only description of the work.
* **It is nevertheless bounded.** Single process, no `fsync` semantics to
  reason about, no range locking, no distributed anything, about 500 lines of
  Python in the reference, and a specification that states every requirement
  the grader checks. An expert who knows the material writes it in about four
  hours, most of it on recovery and checkpoint ordering.

### Expert time estimate (hours)

4

## Oracle & verification

### Oracle strategy

`2873 / 20000 chars`

`solution/solve.sh` copies the reference package over `/app/minikv` and then
imports it, opens a store, runs a transaction and a checkpoint, so a broken
drop-in fails loudly in the oracle step rather than silently in the verifier.

The reference is `solution/minikv/`, about 500 lines across four modules,
standard library only. It scores 1.0000 — 117/117 — in about four seconds.

* `wal.py` — framing shared by both on-disk files. Every record is
  `[u32 payload_len][u32 crc32(payload)][payload]`; a commit payload is
  `[u64 version][u32 count]` followed by `[u32 klen][u32 vlen][key][value]`
  entries, with `vlen == 0xFFFFFFFF` marking a tombstone. `read_records`
  returns the commits it could verify *and the offset just past the last good
  one*, stopping at the first short frame, oversized length, checksum mismatch
  or undecodable payload. That single return value is what gives both the
  prefix property on recovery and the truncation point for reopening a damaged
  log.
* `store.py` — `MiniKV` keeps `_latest` (the current committed value per live
  key) for the fast path and `_versions` (an append-ordered chain of
  `(version, value_or_None)` per key) for snapshot reads. `_commit_version` is
  a monotonic counter; `begin()` records it and registers the snapshot in an
  active-snapshot `Counter`. Commit takes the store lock, checks that no key in
  the write set has a chain entry newer than the snapshot, appends one framed
  record, `flush()`es it, applies it in memory and bumps the counter. Reads at
  the current version hit `_latest`; older snapshots walk the chain.
* `txn.py` — `Transaction` holds only a snapshot number and a write dict, so it
  never holds a lock between calls and readers never block writers. `get`
  checks the write set first, `scan` merges the snapshot view with the write
  set applying tombstones, and any exception from commit aborts and closes the
  transaction.
* Recovery — load `snapshot.dat` if present, replay `wal.log` skipping records
  at or below the checkpoint version, then truncate the log to the last good
  offset before reopening it for append. That last step is what makes a store
  recovered from a damaged log writable again.
* `checkpoint()` — write `snapshot.dat.tmp` (magic plus one framed record
  holding every live key at the current version), `os.replace` it over
  `snapshot.dat`, then truncate `wal.log` back to its 8-byte header. Atomic
  rename first, truncate second, so a crash in between only replays records
  the snapshot already contains. Finally prune version chains below
  `min(checkpoint_version, oldest_open_snapshot)` so open transactions keep
  seeing their snapshot.

Durability is `flush()`, not `fsync()`, matching the stated process-failure
model. Thread safety is a single `RLock` around the store's mutating and
reading paths; transactions hold nothing between calls.

### Verification strategy

`5741 / 20000 chars`

**Visible half.** `/app/tests/test_basic.py` ships in the image: 13 tests over
get/put/delete/scan, reopen, validation and idempotent close. It tells the
agent what "do not regress" means and is something to self-check against. It
is deliberately *not* a description of the target — it covers only behaviour
that already exists — and `instruction.md` says so explicitly.

**Sealed half.** Everything under `tests/` is held out: 117 tests in seven
files, the crash-scenario helper, and all the grading logic. None of it is in
the image the agent works in.

`tests/test.sh` is the entrypoint declared in `task.toml`. It resolves
`IMPL_ROOT` (default `/app`) and `LOG_DIR` (default `/logs`), locates the
sealed suite whichever way the harness laid it out, and calls `grade.py`,
which never executes anything from inside `/app`:

1. **Collect.** Copy `minikv/**/*.py` out of `/app` into a scratch tree the
   grader owns, skipping `__pycache__` and dropping any `conftest.py` found
   inside the package. Nothing outside `minikv/` is copied, so a `conftest.py`,
   `sitecustomize.py`, `pytest.ini` or edited visible test in `/app` has no
   effect. A missing `minikv/__init__.py` is an integrity failure.
2. **Integrity scan.** Tokenise each collected file and inspect `NAME` tokens
   only — comments and string literals are excluded, so documentation is free.
   Referencing `pytest`, `unittest`, `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST`, `sys._getframe`,
   `inspect.currentframe`, `inspect.stack`, `traceback.extract_stack`,
   `sys.argv`, `sys.modules`, `os.environ`, `os.getenv` or the trace hooks
   zeroes the run. Ambiguous words (`stack`, `modules`, `argv`, `environ`)
   only count when qualified by the matching module.
3. **Run.** Copy the grader's pristine tests next to the package and run each
   category as its own pytest process with `cwd` and `PYTHONPATH` pointing at
   the scratch tree, plus `-p no:cacheprovider`, `--rootdir`, `--confcutdir`
   and `--junitxml`. Separate processes mean a deadlock or an infinite loop
   costs one category instead of the run — which matters, because forcing a
   deadlock is the point of one of the isolation tests. Results are parsed
   from JUnit XML, not scraped from stdout.
4. **Budget.** Each category has a wall-clock limit (25–120 s; the reference
   needs under 2 s for any of them) summing to 450 s, and the run as a whole
   has a 480 s deadline inside the bundle's 600 s verifier budget, itself
   inside the draft's 1200 s envelope. Categories run
   cheapest-and-most-diagnostic first, so a submission that hangs late still
   produces a useful report, and reaching the deadline marks the remainder
   unrun rather than killing the verifier.
5. **Report.** Before anything else, delete any pre-existing `reward.txt`,
   `score.txt`, `score.json` or `junit.xml` in `/logs` — the agent can write
   there, and a pre-seeded reward would otherwise be mistaken for this run's
   result. At the end, write the score to `/logs/reward.txt`,
   `/logs/score.txt` and `/logs/score.json` (per-category pass counts,
   per-test failure messages, timings, the weighted score and the verdict),
   and print `SCORE`, `THRESHOLD` and `RESULT`. Exit status is 0 exactly when
   the score reaches the 0.85 threshold.

The seven categories grade the objective from independent angles — public
behaviour, internal invariants under crash, resource bounds, concurrency, and
cost — so a partial or lucky implementation cannot pass:

* `regression` (13) — the grader's own copy of the visible suite. Carries no
  weight of its own; its pass ratio multiplies the final score.
* `api` (25) — types (`str`, `bytearray`, `memoryview`, `int`, `None` all
  rejected on both the store and a transaction), empty-key and size limits,
  "a rejected call changes nothing", `stats()` shape and fields, `wal_bytes`
  agreeing with the real file size, post-`close()` behaviour, both context
  managers, and that the raised exceptions really are the documented classes.
* `isolation` (30) — snapshot reads, the non-blocking `begin()` test, read
  your own writes, invisibility of uncommitted writes, phantom-free `scan`,
  scan/write-set merging, snapshots surviving a checkpoint, atomic commit,
  first-committer-wins in both directions, autocommit-versus-transaction
  conflicts, disjoint writes, read-only transactions never conflicting, write
  skew being allowed, a conflict discarding the entire write set, closed and
  aborted transaction handling, context-manager commit/rollback/conflict
  propagation, and `commit_version` accounting.
* `compaction` (9) — log under 4 KiB and directory under `4L + 65536` after a
  checkpoint over ~15 000 writes, contents preserved across checkpoint and
  reopen, writes after a checkpoint durable, empty-database checkpoint,
  repeated checkpoints stable, `commit_version` unchanged, an all-deleted
  database collapsing to near nothing.
* `threads` (3) — 8 × 400 concurrent autocommit writes all durable and
  recoverable, 8 threads × 100 transactions on disjoint keys with no spurious
  conflicts, and concurrent readers observing a stable 200-key snapshot while
  a writer runs 4 000 updates.
* `durability` (32) — a helper process runs a scenario and `SIGKILL`s itself,
  then the parent reopens and compares: autocommit writes, committed
  transactions, deletes, checkpoint-then-writes, six repetitions of a kill at
  a random instant inside a checkpoint loop, and the negative cases where an
  open or rolled-back transaction must leave no trace. Then eight truncation
  fractions and eight single-byte corruptions, each asserting the prefix
  property, plus write-after-recovery and reopen-preserves-`commit_version`.
* `performance` (5) — the five budgets from the specification.

## Scoring & exploits

### Binary success condition

`951 / 10000 chars`

The weighted score written to `/logs/reward.txt` must reach the
**0.85 pass threshold** declared in `task.toml`, and the integrity scan must
find no violation. `tests/test.sh` exits 0 exactly in that case and 1
otherwise, and prints `SCORE`, `THRESHOLD` and `RESULT` lines.

An integrity violation — a missing `minikv/__init__.py`, or a collected file
that references the test runner, the environment or the call stack — forces
the score to 0.0 and therefore fails regardless of test outcomes.

0.85 is reachable only by implementing the engine, not by covering breadth
cheaply: the two heaviest categories, `durability` (0.28) and `isolation`
(0.27), sum to 0.55, so a submission that skips either cannot clear the bar
even with everything else perfect. The reference scores 1.0000 with 117/117.
The report additionally records `binary_pass`, true only when every one of the
117 tests passes, which is the stricter line the reference actually clears.

### Partial score strategy

`2830 / 10000 chars`

Partial credit is the weighted mean of each scored category's pass ratio, so
the reward is continuous and monotone in how much of the specification is
actually implemented:

| category    | weight | what it measures                                   |
| ----------- | ------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| durability  | 0.28   | crash recovery and damaged-log handling            |
| isolation   | 0.27   | snapshot semantics and conflict detection          |
| performance | 0.17   | the append-only design the budgets force           |
| api         | 0.12   | contract fidelity                                  |
| compaction  | 0.11   | real space reclamation                             |
| threads     | 0.05   | shared-object safety                               |
| regression  | 0.00   | **multiplier** — see below                          |

```
raw   = sum(weight * passed/total) / sum(weight)
score = raw * (regression passed / regression total)
```

rounded to four places.

`regression` deliberately carries no weight of its own. It re-runs the visible
suite, which the untouched starting state already passes; scoring it would
hand the nop run free reward instead of leaving it at its floor. Instead its
pass ratio multiplies the result, so breaking behaviour that already worked
costs proportionally rather than falling off a cliff, and the reward stays
continuous and monotone in both directions.

The scored categories were each audited so that no test in them passes without
some part of the new engine — including the two read benchmarks, which now run
after a `checkpoint()` and through a stale-snapshot transaction respectively.
That is why the untouched state scores 0.0000 while every intermediate stage
of a real attempt still earns credit.

A category that times out or is skipped for lack of verifier time contributes
its full weight to the denominator and zero to the numerator, so hanging is
never cheaper than failing, and a category whose tests fail to collect at all
scores zero rather than being ignored. An integrity violation forces
`score = 0.0` regardless of the rest, and a regression suite that cannot run
at all drives the multiplier to 0.

The score is published to `/logs/reward.txt`, `/logs/score.txt` and
`/logs/score.json`; any pre-existing copy of those files is deleted before
grading starts.

The weighting separates the plausible failure modes rather than collapsing
them: transactions implemented but the whole-file-rewrite persistence kept
lands near 0.50; durability and recovery right but isolation treated as
serializable loses the write-skew and read-only-conflict tests and lands near
0.96; an append-only log with no transactions lands near 0.45. Per-test
failure messages are kept in the report so those cases stay distinguishable
after the fact.

### Anticipated exploits

`5650 / 20000 chars`

* **Detecting the grader.** Reading `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST`, `sys.argv`,
  `sys.modules`, `os.environ`, or walking the call stack to special-case
  behaviour. Countered by the tokenised integrity scan, which zeroes the score
  on any such reference in the collected package, and by the specification
  stating the rule so a legitimate solution has no reason to trip it. Verified
  both ways: a `sys.modules` check trips it, a docstring mentioning `pytest`,
  `os.environ` and `sys.argv` does not.
* **Shipping code the grader was not meant to run.** A `conftest.py` that
  monkeypatches assertions, a `sitecustomize.py` executed at interpreter
  start, a `pytest.ini` that deselects tests, or edits to the visible
  `tests/test_basic.py`. Countered by copying only `minikv/**/*.py` into a
  grader-owned tree, dropping any `conftest.py` from inside the package,
  grading against the grader's own copy of the visible suite, and running
  pytest with `--rootdir`, `--confcutdir` and `-p no:cacheprovider`.
* **Overfitting the visible tests.** The shipped suite is the floor, not the
  target: it describes only what the store already does, and passing it is
  worth zero — it multiplies, it does not add. The 117 decisive cases are sealed in
  `tests/` and never enter the image.
* **Faking durability by writing on `close()`.** Every crash scenario ends in
  `SIGKILL`, so no `close()`, no `atexit`, no `__del__` and no finaliser ever
  runs. The parent additionally asserts the child died with signal 9, so a
  child that exits cleanly — by catching the kill, or by forking a survivor —
  fails the test instead of passing it. The checkpoint-race scenario guards
  its loop for the same reason: if `checkpoint()` raises, the child exits with
  a status that is not signal 9, so a store with no `checkpoint()` cannot pass
  on the strength of an armed timer firing during interpreter shutdown.
* **Faking snapshots with a lock.** Holding a lock from `begin()` to
  `commit()` makes concurrent tests look isolated. The isolation tests are
  single-threaded and interleave autocommit writes between `begin()` and the
  read, so a held lock deadlocks and the category times out to zero.
* **Reaching for serializability instead.** Validating the read set makes
  "isolation" sound stronger and passes the lost-update tests, but
  `test_write_skew_is_allowed` asserts that the classic write-skew pair *both*
  commit, and `test_read_only_transaction_never_conflicts` asserts a read-only
  transaction always commits. Over-strictness is penalised as precisely as
  under-strictness.
* **Hardcoding the fixtures.** Keys and values are generated, the performance
  fixture uses 20 000 keys, and the crash scenarios live in a sealed helper.
  There is no small fixed answer set to memorise.
* **Passing recovery by discarding the log.** Returning an empty database
  after any damage satisfies the prefix property vacuously — so the suite also
  asserts that a clean reopen sees all ten commits, that truncating one byte
  leaves strictly fewer than ten (the tail really is lost, not the whole log),
  and that a store recovered from a damaged log accepts new writes that are
  still there after another reopen.
* **Resynchronising past a corrupt record.** Scanning forward for the next
  valid-looking frame recovers "more" data and feels generous, but it
  resurrects commits that must be invisible; the prefix assertion rejects any
  gap in the recovered key sequence, and each surviving value is checked
  against the key it belongs to.
* **Keeping the data somewhere other than the log.** The specification
  requires `wal.log` to be the mechanism by which committed data reaches disk,
  and the crash tests assert the file exists after recovery, so the naive
  whole-file rewrite cannot collect durability credit.
* **`checkpoint()` as a no-op, or as a log copy.** Countered by two bounds
  that must hold simultaneously: `wal.log` at most 4 KiB, and the whole
  directory at most `4L + 65536` bytes after ~15 000 writes collapse to 2 000
  live keys — a copy of the log fails the second, a no-op fails the first, and
  the all-deleted test requires the directory to collapse below 64 KiB.
* **Checkpointing on every commit** to keep the log trivially small. Legal,
  but it makes every write O(live set) and misses the 20 000-put budget by a
  wide margin.
* **Keeping everything in memory and writing once at the end.** Fails every
  `SIGKILL` scenario, and `test_reopen_is_not_quadratic` forces recovery of a
  10 000-commit log to stay linear.
* **Weakening the API to dodge tests.** Accepting `str` keys, returning `None`
  instead of raising, or redefining `ConflictError` as something looser. The
  `api` category pins types, exception identity and the hierarchy, asserts the
  classes are the ones actually raised on a real conflict, and asserts that a
  rejected call leaves `commit_version` and the visible state untouched.
* **Pre-writing the reward.** The agent can write to `/logs`, so leaving a
  `reward.txt` containing `1.0` would be scored without solving anything.
  `grade.py` deletes every reward artefact in `/logs` and beside itself before
  the first category runs, so only this run's number survives.
* **Editing or deleting the instructions, the README or the visible tests** to
  make `/app` look finished. None of those files is read by the grader; only
  `minikv/**/*.py` is collected.
* **Attempting to install a dependency or reach the network.** The rollout is
  sealed and there is no package index; only the standard library is
  importable, and an `ImportError` at collection time fails every category
  rather than one.

### Network requirements

**Mode:** none

**Hosts:** _(none)_

**Justification:**

The task is fully offline. Python 3.11, git and pytest are baked into the
image at build time, the store is standard-library-only by specification,
and every graded workload is generated inside the sandbox. Nothing the agent
or the verifier does needs to leave the container, which also makes grading
deterministic.

## Authoring notes

_Not a form field._

Not a draft field. Authoring notes.

* Measured on this machine: oracle 1.0000 (117/117, ~4 s), nop 0.0000. The
  whole verifier run for a correct submission is about four seconds against a
  1200 s timeout.
* `verifierTimeoutSec` is the form's default 1200. An earlier revision raised
  it to 2400 in this file and in `task.toml`, and the bundle was rejected with
  "verifier timeout exceeds draft" — the platform compares `task.toml` against
  the draft it stored, and the raised value evidently never reached it. The
  lesson is in CLAUDE.md rule 3: the bundle's asks must hold against the draft
  as submitted, which you cannot read back from this repository, so do not
  exceed the form defaults without a reason. `grade.py` enforces its own 900 s
  deadline inside the 1200 s, and the per-category limits (60–420 s) may sum
  above it — the deadline absorbs that by design, marking later categories
  unrun rather than letting the harness kill the verifier.
* Trial budget: agent 14400 s + verifier 1200 s + build (~2 min) is well
  inside the 50 400 s per-trial ceiling, and `agentTimeoutSec` clears the
  7200 s long-horizon floor.
* `[environment] network_mode = "open"` in `task.toml` is the *build* phase,
  which the guideline says is not gated; the rollout and the verifier are both
  `none`. This is the one value in the bundle that could not be checked
  against a published enum — flagged here rather than assumed correct.
* `regression` was moved to weight 0 and turned into a score multiplier after
  measuring that the untouched workspace scored 0.1785 with it weighted. Three
  other sources of free credit were closed at the same time: a checkpoint-race
  scenario that passed on a store with no `checkpoint()` (an armed timer fired
  during interpreter shutdown after the loop had already raised), four `api`
  tests that never touched the transactional API, and two throughput
  benchmarks that measured only reads the naive store was already fast at.
  Together those took the nop from 0.1785 to 0.0000.
* The image build is **unverified**: this authoring environment has the docker
  CLI but no daemon. The Dockerfile is deliberately conservative because of
  that — the build-time self-check lives in `environment/selfcheck.py` rather
  than a `RUN` heredoc, which the classic Dockerfile parser does not join
  across newlines. `selfcheck.py` was run directly against both the seed (it
  passes) and the reference (it correctly refuses). Build the image once
  before submitting.
* `bundle/environment/tests/test_basic.py` and `bundle/tests/test_regression.py`
  must stay identical below their docstrings — the second is the sealed copy
  the grader runs. Diff them after touching either.
